title: Models, effort and cost

story: The first pilot week's bill arrives, and two lines stand out. The readiness check, which only reads a ticket and answers ready, ask or hand back, cost almost as much per run as planning, because every step ran on the strongest model at high effort. And one run of Nova cost three times the others: a step failed, the harness restarted the session at a higher effort, and the new session paid again for the 80,000 tokens of system prompt, tools and conversation that the old session had already paid for.
Nobody wants a cheap agent that fails. But paying the top price for every small job, and paying twice for the same tokens, buys nothing.
hook.question: How do I give each job the model and effort it needs, and stop paying twice for the same tokens?

read.h: A model and an effort for each job
p: Two settings decide most of what a step costs. The model is the obvious one: Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, Sonnet 5.5 half of that, and Haiku 5.5 a small fraction. The second is effort, a setting on the model that says how much it should think before and while it answers: low, medium, high, xhigh or max. Higher effort means more thinking tokens, which are paid as output, and usually better work on hard problems. Opus 5.5's default effort on the API is medium.

So we route by job. A job is the kind of work a step does: reading a ticket, planning, building, searching code, fixing CI. A small table maps each job to a model and an effort, and any job that is not listed falls back to building, Opus at medium. Fixing CI can run at low effort, because CI itself checks the result. These are starting values; measuring on our own tickets decides the final numbers.

notes.text: Reading a ticket and giving a verdict: a mid-size model, little thinking.
Helpers read and search and return pointers: the cheapest model is enough.
CI is the checker, so a fix can start at low effort and go up only if CI stays red.
Anything unknown gets the build route, Opus at medium.
No maxTurns, no maxBudgetUsd, no taskBudget. A test keeps it that way.

read.h: Do not pay twice: the prompt cache
p: Every request of a session sends the whole prefix again: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the conversation so far. On a long run that prefix is tens of thousands of tokens on every turn. Prompt caching makes the repeats cheap. The API stores the prefix for a while, and a later request that starts with exactly the same tokens reads it from the cache. On Opus 5.5 a cache read costs 5% of the normal input price. Writing the cache costs a bit more than normal input: 1.25 times for a cache that lives 5 minutes, 2 times for one that lives an hour. modelUsage shows both, as cacheCreationInputTokens and cacheReadInputTokens.

The cache only helps while the prefix stays the same and the cache is alive. A new session builds a new conversation, so the old conversation's cache is useless. That is the expensive line in the story. When a step fails, we keep the session and raise the effort for the next turn with applyFlagSettings(), then send the retry as a new message. This needs a session with streaming input, where the prompt is a stream of messages you keep feeding, not a single string.

How long the cache lives matters too. CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL takes 5m or 1h, the only two values. An agent that waits for people between turns, like Nova after a question, needs the hour, or the cache is gone when the answer arrives. A routine that never waits should keep 5 minutes, because hour-long cache writes cost more.

notes.text: In streaming input mode, you send messages as an async iterable of user messages.
Raise the effort for the next turn of the running session. No restart, so the prefix stays the same.
The retry is just another message in the same conversation.

read.see:
no cache at all   $0.3420
cache write (5m)  $0.4220
cache write (1h)  $0.6620
cache read        $0.0380

read.h: No limits that cut work in half
p: The options type offers maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd and taskBudget. They look like safety, but each one fires in the middle of the work: the session stops at turn 30 or at five dollars, with a half-edited repo and a plan half done, and everything spent so far is wasted. We never set them. Cost is guided instead: the right model and effort per job, a warm cache, check-ins when a step runs far past its estimate, and a far-away spending backstop that acts only between turns. A test fails the build if a limit ever appears in the options, so nobody adds one "to be safe".

The last setting that touches cost is where the requests go. In the VM there is no API key. The env option points the claude process at our gateway instead, which adds the real key and records every call with the run's tags. Remember that env replaces the child's whole environment, so always spread process.env first.

code.file: the env of a session in the VM
code.text:
env: {
  ...process.env, // env REPLACES the child's environment: keep PATH and HOME
  ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: GATEWAY_URL, // every model call goes to our gateway
  ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN: runToken, // sent as a Bearer token; not an Anthropic key, dies with the run
  ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS: "x-ai-agents-step: build", // one "Name: value" per line
  CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL: "1h", // Nova waits on people; routines use 5m
},

notes.text: Without this spread the claude process has no PATH and no HOME, and fails in confusing ways.
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN goes into the Authorization header. The gateway checks it and adds the real key.
Extra headers on every request, so the gateway can split the bill by step.

deeper.h: Go deeper: effort is not the same as a thinking budget
p: Current models think adaptively: they decide how much to think, steered by effort. The older thinking setting with a fixed token budget is a separate, older control, and the SDK's thinking option still accepts it for older models. For our models, effort is the knob.

Behind a gateway, Claude Code disables MCP tool search by default, because a proxy may not pass its special blocks through. Our harness turns it back on with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, because our gateway forwards them.

lab.title: Route a job, guard the limits, price the cache
needs: For one step only: your own Anthropic API key
lab.goal: Write a routing table with tests that forbid limits, compute what the prompt cache saves on one long turn, and read the cache numbers of a real session.

guess.q: A turn sends 80,000 tokens of unchanged prefix plus 1,500 new tokens to Opus 5.5 and gets 800 tokens back. Roughly how much cheaper is it when the prefix is read from the cache instead of sent without caching?

options.why: Cache reads on Opus 5.5 cost 5% of the input price, and the prefix is almost all of the input. The saving is far bigger.
Without a cache the turn costs about $0.34; with a cache read about $0.04. The lab computes it.

options.text: The same, because output tokens are what cost money
options.why: Output costs more per token, but here there are 800 output tokens against 80,000 input tokens.

cache-math prints the four prices, and the cache read line is about a ninth of the no-cache line.
With your key, the second cache-check run shows a bigger cache read than the first.
Your step-env tests pass, and a misspelled step such as "bulid" fails npx tsc.
lab.fix: After a failed step, the harness closes the session and starts a new one with effort high and the same task text. Every retry costs about as much as the first attempt, and Nova sometimes asks Sean a question it already asked. Explain both symptoms with what you learned about sessions and the cache, and change the retry so it stays in the same session.
explain: What do the model and the effort each change about a step's cost and quality?
Why does restarting a session at a higher effort cost more than raising the effort inside the running session?
Why does Nova use a one-hour cache and a CI-fixing routine a five-minute cache?
lab.done: Your routing table is tested, nobody can add a limit by accident, and you can read cache writes and reads in modelUsage and say what they cost.

check.q: A step's checks fail. What is the cheapest way to try once more with more thinking?

options.text: Start a new session with effort high and the same task
options.why: A new session builds its conversation again and cannot use the old cache, so it pays for the whole prefix again.

options.text: Raise the effort with applyFlagSettings in the running session and send the retry as a new message
options.why: The session's prefix stays the same, so most of it is read from the cache, and the model keeps everything it learned.

options.text: Switch the whole run to the strongest model at max effort
options.why: That raises the price of every later step too. Go one level up for this step only.

check.q: Why do we never set maxTurns or maxBudgetUsd on an agent session?

options.text: They fire in the middle of the work and throw away what was done so far
options.why: A limit stops a half-finished step. We guide cost with routing, the cache, check-ins and a backstop between turns.

options.text: The SDK ignores them in dontAsk mode
options.why: They work in every mode. That is exactly why they are dangerous.
They are supported options. We choose not to use them.

check.q: Nova asks Sean a question and the answer comes 20 minutes later. Which cache setting fits?

options.why: The cache would expire before the answer arrives, and the whole prefix would be written again.
Every turn would pay full price for tens of thousands of prefix tokens.

options.text: 1h, because the session waits on a person between turns
options.why: One-hour writes cost more, but they survive the wait. Routines that never wait keep 5m.

p: The harness's routing table is this lesson's table: readiness on Sonnet 5.5 at low, planning and building on Opus 5.5 at medium (planning goes to high for fuzzy tickets), helpers on Haiku 5.5 at medium, QA on Sonnet 5.5 at medium, and CI and dependency fixers on Opus at low. A failed step is re-run once, one level up, in the same session, and then left to the progress watcher. Nova and the bug fixers use a one-hour cache; routines use five minutes. A test fails the build if maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd or taskBudget ever appear.

In every VM the env points ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at the LLM gateway and puts the run's token in ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, so no API key is ever on the machine. Each step's session adds OpenTelemetry tags and a step header, so Grafana can show what each step of RH-1234 cost. The check-ins and the far-away backstop, which act only between turns, live in the harness.

tickets.why: routing.ts, the one-level-up retry in the same session, the cache TTL and the no-limits test.
stepEnv: the OpenTelemetry tags and the step header for every session.
The gateway and its run token, which replace the API key in the VM.
Check-ins past the estimate and the far-away cost backstop, between turns only.

words.plain: How much the model thinks before and while it answers: low, medium, high, xhigh or max.
Our map from a kind of job to a model and an effort, with build as the fallback.
The API's stored copy of a request's prefix; a later request with the same prefix reads it cheaply.
How long the cache lives: 5 minutes or 1 hour. Longer costs more to write.
A session whose prompt is a stream of messages you keep feeding, so you can add turns and change settings.

review.q: Price one turn from memory: 80,000 cached prefix tokens read, 1,500 new input tokens and 800 output tokens on Opus 5.5.
What does env replace, and what do you always put first?
review.a: The claude process's whole environment; spread process.env first, then the gateway URL, the run token and the headers.

remember: Give each job its model and effort, keep failed steps in the same session so the cache stays warm, and never set a limit that cuts work in half.
